lesson_title: Why Old Festive Lights All Went Dark Together
hook_text: One bulb blows and the whole string goes dark. Blame the series circuit.
clip_script: Remember old festive lights, where one dead bulb made the whole string go dark? They were wired in series: every bulb on one single loop, one after the other. In a series circuit there is only one road for the current, so break it anywhere and everything stops. Three rules make series circuits easy. One: the current is the same everywhere. An ammeter before, between or after the bulbs shows the same number, because nothing gets used up. Two: the battery's voltage is shared. Two identical bulbs on a 6 volt battery get 3 volts each, and the shares always add back up to 6. Three: every bulb you add makes the road harder, so the current drops and all the bulbs get dimmer. That is why your house is never wired in series. But a fuse always is, so it can cut everything off at once.
visual_style: A string of old festive lights going dark; a single-loop circuit with ammeters all showing 0,2; voltmeters showing 3 and 3 adding to 6; bulbs dimming as more are added.
mood: Nostalgic hook, then crisp and logical.
pacing: Story opening, three quick rules with a beat on each, a punchy finish on the fuse.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and predict ammeter readings in series circuits.
